sources.ref_file_title: KOS16 - MASCOT Faster Malicious Arithmetic Secure Computation with Oblivious Transfer
sources.authors: Marcel Keller, Emmanuela Orsini, Peter Scholl
sources.note: Verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib: cryptobib_key CCS:KelOrsSch16, pages 830-842, doi 10.1145/2976749.2978357; eprint entry EPRINT:KelOrsSch16 confirms https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/505. MASCOT instantiates the SPDZ preprocessing phase (authenticated multiplication triples) from OT extension instead of somewhat-homomorphic encryption.

pages.class_justification: MASCOT is a UC protocol proven in a hybrid model with an OT (extension) functionality; neither the paper nor any follow-up classifies the construction in the RTV04 taxonomy, and protocol-completeness results do not map cleanly onto it. Left unstated rather than guessed.
pages.model_justification: The hypothesis is the OT-extension functionality itself; given it, MASCOT's remaining ingredients are symmetric-key operations and commitment/coin-tossing functionalities. No idealized model is assumed on top of the hypothesis in the statement of the result, but see flags: instantiating the auxiliary functionalities in practice may use a random oracle.
pages.statement: SPDZ-style [[secure-multi-party-computation#mpc-with-preprocessing-spdz-etc|MPC with preprocessing]] can base its offline phase entirely on [[oblivious-transfer#ot-extension|OT extension]]: the MASCOT protocol generates SPDZ's authenticated multiplication triples from correlated OT extension and symmetric-key operations alone, yielding maliciously secure dishonest-majority MPC for arithmetic circuits with a fast information-theoretic online phase and no homomorphic encryption — [[KOS16 - MASCOT Faster Malicious Arithmetic Secure Computation with Oblivious Transfer|KOS16]].
pages.sketch: Each cross term of a secret-shared multiplication triple is computed pairwise by correlated OT on the bit decomposition of one party's share (Gilboa-style oblivious product evaluation); shares and triples are then authenticated with SPDZ-style information-theoretic MACs whose keys are also distributed via correlated OT, and sacrificing plus combining steps remove errors a malicious party can inject. The online phase consumes one triple per multiplication as in SPDZ.
notes_to_keep: The hypothesis `ot-extension` has no dedicated page (it is a section of [[oblivious-transfer]]), and the conclusion `mpc-with-preprocessing` is a section of [[secure-multi-party-computation]].
flags: Precursor worth a look: TinyOT (Nielsen-Nordholt-Orlandi-Burra, CRYPTO 2012, cryptobib C:NNOB12, eprint 2011/091) instantiated preprocessing from OT extension earlier, for two-party boolean circuits; MASCOT is cited as original because the page's conclusion names SPDZ-style (arithmetic, multiparty) preprocessing. The verifier may want NNOB12 as a second source or a separate edge.

The homomorphic-encryption branch of the migrated disjunctive bullet (SPDZ proper, i.e. Damgard-Pastro-Smart-Zakarias, CRYPTO 2012) is a separate record per the migration note; DPSZ12 has no reference page yet and is not required by this edge.
MASCOT's UC proof uses auxiliary commitment/random-coin functionalities; whether their instantiation needs a random oracle should be checked before tightening `model` beyond `standard`.

sources.ref_file_title: HILL99 - A Pseudorandom Generator from Any One-Way Function
sources.authors: Johan Hastad, Russell Impagliazzo, Leonid A. Levin, Michael Luby
sources.note: Already a wiki reference; the general OWF-to-PRG construction.

sources.ref_file_title: GL89 - A Hard-Core Predicate for All One-Way Functions
sources.note: Component, not an independent proof of the edge: supplies the hard-core predicate used inside HILL99, and directly gives the one-bit-stretch PRG from a one-way PERMUTATION.

sources.ref_file_title: HRV10 - Efficiency improvements in constructing pseudorandom generators from one-way functions
sources.authors: Iftach Haitner, Omer Reingold, Salil P. Vadhan
sources.note: Verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib: cryptobib_key STOC:HaiReiVad10, pages 437-446. Introduces next-block pseudoentropy; seed length ~O(n^4).

sources.ref_file_title: VZ12 - Characterizing pseudoentropy and simplifying pseudorandom generator constructions
sources.authors: Salil P. Vadhan, Colin Jia Zheng
sources.note: Verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib: cryptobib_key STOC:VadZhe12, pages 817-836. Simplifies the construction and reduces seed length to ~O(n^3).

pages.class_justification: The HILL construction evaluates the one-way function only as an oracle (its outputs are hashed and fed to the Goldreich-Levin predicate), and the security proof exhibits one fixed reduction that runs any PRG distinguisher as an oracle to invert the function. This is the RTV04 fully-black-box shape; the black-box efficiency literature (HRV10, and the Holenstein-Sinha lower bound on black-box constructions of PRGs from OWFs) treats HILL as the canonical fully-black-box construction.
pages.statement: Any [[hash-function#preimage-resistance-one-wayness|one-way function]] suffices to construct a [[pseudorandom-generator|PRG]] — [[HILL99 - A Pseudorandom Generator from Any One-Way Function|HILL99]]. The construction extracts the computational entropy of the one-way function via universal hashing and the [[GL89 - A Hard-Core Predicate for All One-Way Functions|GL89]] hard-core predicate; for a one-way permutation $f$ the one-bit-stretch generator $G(x, r) = (f(x), r, \langle x, r \rangle)$ is already a PRG.
pages.sketch: The Goldreich-Levin bit creates a computational entropy gap: $(f(x), r, \langle x, r \rangle)$ is indistinguishable from a distribution whose entropy exceeds its real entropy. Taking many independent copies, flattening with universal hashing, and extracting turns this gap into genuine stretch; a hybrid argument converts any distinguisher into an inverter for $f$.
pages.improvements_text:
- Seed length reduced to $\tilde{O}(n^4)$ via the notion of next-block pseudoentropy — [[HRV10 - Efficiency improvements in constructing pseudorandom generators from one-way functions|HRV10]]
- Seed length $\tilde{O}(n^3)$, with a simplified analysis characterizing pseudoentropy in terms of KL-hardness of sampling — [[VZ12 - Characterizing pseudoentropy and simplifying pseudorandom generator constructions|VZ12]]
notes_to_keep: The converse also holds — any PRG is a one-way function, since the seed is a preimage of the output — so OWF $\Leftrightarrow$ PRG. The converse direction is its own hyperedge ([[prg-to-hash-function]]) and is not covered by this page.

The hypothesis `owf` is the one-wayness notion defined at [[hash-function#preimage-resistance-one-wayness]]. That definition is _keyed_ and implicitly compressing, whereas HILL99 is stated for unkeyed one-way functions — see the note on [[hash-function|Hash functions]].

The two pages should be merged or one deprecated; my class/statement determination applies to both.
Kind is implication and should stay so: the converse PRG => OWF exists as its own page (prg-to-hash-function.md), so per the instructions neither page becomes an equivalence.

pages.class_justification: Degenerate fully-black-box shape: the construction is the identity (the permutation itself is the one-way function), so it uses the hypothesis only as an oracle, and the security reduction forwards any inverter of the function verbatim as an inverter of the permutation, using it only as an oracle.
pages.statement: Every [[one-way-permutation|OWP]] is a [[hash-function#preimage-resistance-one-wayness|one-way function]]: the identity construction preserves one-wayness, since any algorithm inverting the function with noticeable probability inverts the permutation with the same probability — folklore.
notes_to_keep: Wikilink target surprise: OWF resolves to `[[hash-function]]`, the page that also holds CRHF/collision resistance. The migration will conflate OWF with CRHF unless hash-function is split into distinct objects.
flags: Definitional mismatch worth recording on the page: the wiki's one-wayness notion at hash-function#preimage-resistance-one-wayness is keyed and implicitly compressing, while a permutation is unkeyed and length-preserving; the trivial implication is for the plain (unkeyed, non-compressing) OWF notion. Same caveat as on owf-to-prg-hill99.
The converse fails in the black-box setting (OWFs do not black-box imply OWPs; cf. Rudich's separation and MM11 for injective OWFs), so kind: implication is right.

pages.statement: [[polynomial-time|P]] $\subseteq$ [[bounded-error-probabilistic-polynomial-time|BPP]]: a deterministic polynomial-time machine is a probabilistic polynomial-time machine that ignores its random tape and errs with probability $0$ — folklore.
flags: Transitively redundant with the chain p-to-zpp, zpp-to-rp, rp-to-bpp (as the migration note observed); whether to keep the direct edge alongside the chain is an editorial call for the graph model.

pages.statement: [[polynomial-time|P]] $\subseteq$ [[co-nondeterministic-polynomial-time|coNP]]: P is closed under complement, so for $L \in \classP$ the complement $\bar{L}$ lies in $\classP \subseteq \classNP$, placing $L$ in $\classcoNP$ — folklore.

pages.class_justification: Proven unconditional containment between complexity classes; per repo convention proven inclusions take class: free.
pages.statement: [[polynomial-time|P]] $\subseteq$ [[nondeterministic-polynomial-time|NP]]: a polynomial-time decider is a polynomial-time verifier that ignores its certificate — equivalently, a nondeterministic machine that makes no nondeterministic choices — folklore.

pages.class_justification: Proven unconditional containment between complexity classes; per repo convention proven inclusions take class: free.
pages.statement: [[polynomial-time|P]] $\subseteq$ [[p-poly|P/poly]]: the standard tableau simulation converts a Turing machine running in time $t(n)$ into a circuit of size $O(t(n)^2)$ for each input length, so a polynomial-time machine yields a polynomial-size circuit family; equivalently, a P machine decides its language with empty advice — folklore.

pages.class_justification: Proven unconditional containment between complexity classes; per repo convention proven inclusions take class: free.
pages.statement: [[polynomial-time|P]] $\subseteq$ [[randomized-polynomial-time|RP]]: a deterministic polynomial-time machine, viewed as a probabilistic machine that ignores its randomness, accepts every yes-instance with probability $1$ and every no-instance with probability $0$, meeting RP's one-sided-error condition — folklore.

pages.class_justification: Proven unconditional containment between complexity classes; per repo convention proven inclusions take class: free.
pages.statement: [[polynomial-time|P]] $\subseteq$ [[zero-error-probabilistic-polynomial-time|ZPP]]: a deterministic polynomial-time machine is a Las Vegas machine that never errs and whose expected running time equals its worst-case polynomial running time — folklore.

sources.ref_file_title: GHJS25 - Public-Key Encryption from Planted Clique and Noisy k-LIN Over Expanders
sources.authors: Riddhi Ghosal, Isaac M. Hair, Aayush Jain, Amit Sahai
sources.note: Wiki reference page confirms Theorem 8.8: an alternative PKE construction based on a search variant of the noisy k-LIN assumption, jointly with planted clique.

pages.class_justification: GHJS25 give a concrete construction with a standard security reduction but do not place it in the RTV04 taxonomy; the hypotheses are assumptions rather than primitives, so the fully-black-box shape is not directly attested. Left unstated.
pages.model_justification: The paper's constructions are in the standard model; the abstract states plain semantic security against polynomial-size adversaries with no idealized model.
pages.statement: Semantically secure [[public-key-encryption|PKE]] exists assuming the joint hardness of [[planted-clique|planted clique]] and the search variant of [[noisy-k-lin-over-expanders#search-noisy-k-lin|noisy $k$-LIN over expanders]], in which the adversary must recover $\mathbf{s}$ from $(\mathbf{M}, \mathbf{M}\mathbf{s}+\mathbf{e})$ for an expanding sparse matrix $\mathbf{M}$ — [[GHJS25 - Public-Key Encryption from Planted Clique and Noisy k-LIN Over Expanders|GHJS25]], Theorem 8.8. This is an alternative to the paper's main construction from the decisional variant (Theorem 5.12); the search-to-decision reduction known for standard LPN does not immediately transfer to the expanding-matrix setting, so the two hypotheses are recorded separately.
flags: The page's Notes contain a migration serialization bug: 'Citations disagree across pages: [object Object]'. All three migrated statements in fact cite GHJS25 Theorem 8.8 consistently; the line can be dropped.

The hypothesis search-noisy-k-lin is a section-level sub-object of noisy-k-lin-over-expanders with no page of its own; the sibling edge from the decisional variant (Theorem 5.12) should exist as a separate hyperedge — verify it does.

The wiki's GHJS25 reference page abstract writes the planted clique size as $n^{\log^\alpha n}$, which is super-polynomial and almost certainly a typo for a quasi-polynomially small clique (cf. the $2^{(\log n)^\alpha}$ expander parameter in the same sentence); worth a skeptical-checker look at the reference page, not this edge.
